paper_title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.

Introduction Streaming video understanding requires answering questions about an ongoing video stream using only observations available at query time [21, 31]. In this single-pass setting, the system has limited space to store frames and must decide what to preserve before it knows which details future question will require. We use the term streaming harness for the policies that maintain this memory and reFigure 1. From manual design to open-world harness evolution. (a) Researchers design and revise the memory and retrieval pipelines of streaming systems [8, 54, 57, 63]. (b) Video recursive self-improvement (RSI) methods [22, 24, 26] automate harness revision from execution feedback within preconfigured set of models and tools. (c) MORSE makes online research part of this loop. An LLM-based Editor investigates observed failures through papers, model cards, and code, then adapts existing methods and requests missing perception tools. Host-reviewed tool acquisition lets the harness and its available capabilities evolve together around frozen answering VLM. trieve evidence for video-language model (VLM) [22]. As frames arrive, its write policy selects which observations to retain and how to represent and organize them in memory. When question arrives, its read policy uses the question to retrieve relevant evidence and assemble the context for the VLM. These policies must be designed together. The write policy determines which details remain available, and even retained detail can help answer question only if the read policy can locate it within the latency budget. As illustrated in Figure 1(a), existing streaming systems use researcher-designed policies for memory compression, temporal organization, and query-aware retrieval [8, 54, 57, 63]. Recent recursive self-improvement (RSI) methods automate parts of this design process by analyzing failures and revising the harness code [22, 24, 26]. In the loop shown in Figure 1(b), the editor draws on its prior knowledge to devise revisions using predefined set of models and tools. However, this limits the search to solutions the editor can recall or develop on its own. Faced with failure that recurs across videos, human researcher would consult the literature to see whether others have already addressed the underlying problem. Even work on different task may offer method to adapt or pretrained model that provides capability the harness lacks. An editor could follow the same approach, using the failures it diagnoses to guide an online search for solutions it can adapt to the harness. Motivated by this, we introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that lets an editor read papers online and adapt relevant methods to its own streaming video harness.1 Specifically, MORSE has two roles. The streaming Solver executes the harness, updating memory as frames arrive and retrieving evidence for frozen VLM when question is asked. The LLM-based Editor inspects the Solvers training traces, identifies recurring failures, and searches papers, model pages, and code for approaches that address their causes. It translates its findings into changes to the memory and retrieval policies. When failure calls for new perceptual capability, it can request pretrained model and adapt these policies to use its outputs after review and integration. As shown in Figure 1(c), online research informs both program revisions and the expansion of available perception tools, allowing the policies and capabilities to evolve together. Held-out validation guides two stages of evolution: first improving answer quality, then reducing answer latency while bounding quality loss. Both stages enforce answer-latency and write-load limits, and the selected harness becomes the starting point for the next round. Starting from simple harness, MORSE improves held-out validation accuracy from 68.3% to 79.4% through recursive evolution. On held-out test benchmarks with the final harness achieves 75.1% on Qwen3-VL-8B, OVO-Bench (RT+BT), 78.9% on StreamingBench, and 71.6% on StreamBench, exceeding the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone by 3.1, 2.7, and 6.3 1To prevent evaluation data leakage, we block online access to benchmark data and answers and exclude tools trained or fine-tuned on evaluation videos or annotations. percentage points, respectively. These gains span backward tracing, contextual reasoning, and memory search. Beyond accuracy, MORSE answers 6.0 and 3.5 faster than MemEvo and OASIS. Its harness transfers unchanged to LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B without further evolution. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce MORSE, an open-world auto-research framework that uses streaming memory failures to guide online research, enabling recursive improvements beyond predefined designs and capabilities. We expand the search space of harness evolution from program code to perceptual capabilities, so that memory and retrieval policies evolve together with the perception tools they use while the answering VLM stays frozen. Experiments on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamBench show that MORSE outperforms existing streaming methods and harness RSI baselines across answering models, and ablations quantify the contribution of external research and of the expanded capability space. 2. Related Work Streaming Video Understanding. Streaming video understanding requires systems to preserve useful history as frames arrive and retrieve evidence when question is posed, without access to future observations. Existing methods address these demands through two complementary directions. Training-based systems learn continuous interaction and memory mechanisms within the model [6, 61, 66]. Inference-time approaches build on existing backbones by designing how evidence is stored and accessed: StreamMem and FluxMem compress or organize visual history [54, 57], while ReKV and StreamScout retrieve cached representations or acquire query-relevant evidence [8, 63]. These methods offer different trade-offs between retaining history and answering efficiently, but their overall memory structures and processing pipelines are specified by researchers, even when individual decisions are adaptive or learned. MORSE automates the design of these policies, using observed failures to revise an executable memory and retrieval program around frozen answering model. Harness Recursive Self-Improvement. Recursive selfimprovement turns evaluation feedback into program changes that persist beyond an individual task. LLMguided evolution applies this principle to executable programs, agent workflows, and memory architectures through repeated proposal, evaluation, and selection [12, 32, 65, 69]. For video understanding, recent methods evolve contextconstruction and tool-use programs around frozen perception models [56, 59], with failure diagnosis and controlled feedback guiding the search for more generalizable harness revisions [22, 26]. Test-time latency and write cost are measured on single NVIDIA H100 GPU. 4.2. Main Results Results on OVO-Bench. MORSE achieves the highest overall accuracy within all three backbone groups in Table 1. With Qwen3-VL-8B, it reaches 75.1%, ahead of the manually designed StreamScout at 69.7% and the evolved MemEvo program at 72.0%. The task breakdown helps explain this advantage. Relative to MemEvo, the margin is larger on backward tracing than on real-time perception, indicating that better use of past observations is an important source of improvement. The same pattern holds with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, where backward-tracing accuracy reaches 60.5%, 7.9 points above the best competing score on this subset. With Qwen3.8-27B, the larger advantage over FluxMem, the strongest competing harness overall, is instead in real-time perception. Harness evolution benefits different model sizes and temporal tasks, although the capabilities that improve most differ across backbones. Results on StreamingBench and StreamBench. As shown in Table 2, MORSE achieves the highest average score within all three backbone groups on both benchmarks. On StreamingBench, Qwen3-VL-8B improves all four subsets over MemEvo. The gains on anomaly and misleading context understanding suggest that the evolved harness supplies useful historical evidence for interpreting current observations. On StreamBench, the same backbone reaches 71.6%, compared with 65.3% for StreamScout, the strongest competing harness. It leads in four of six categories, with clear advantages in object search and short-term memory search. These results support the usefulness of the evolved memory and retrieval policies for both contextual reasoning and free-form answers, beyond the multiple-choice format used during evolution. With this backbone, other harnesses remain stronger on conversational interaction and knowledge-based questions. The advantage also holds in domain absent from evolution: on the driving videos of ODV-Bench [61], MORSE reaches 67.1% with Qwen3-VL-8B, compared with 62.6% for MemEvo and 58.6% for the model alone (Sec. We separate the contribution of consulting external resources from that of expanding the available tools. Starting from the same seed H0, we repeat evolution with Qwen3-VL-8B under the same data splits, round and candidate budgets, and gates. Without online research, the Editor can still request tools from its prior knowledge, subject to host review. Without tool requests, it can still read papers, model cards, and code, but must build every candidate from the initial inventory T0. As shown in Table 4, removing online research lowers OVO-Bench accuracy from 75.1% to 72.9% even though 8 show improvements over competing harnesses across answering models, and the OVO-Bench efficiency evaluation shows lower answer latency than MemEvo and OASIS. The evolution analysis illustrates how capabilities introduced to address failures can later be reorganized to reduce computation. These findings support practical approach to recursive self-improvement: learning when and how to reuse published methods and models, with validation determining which changes benefit the harness.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: This supplementary material describes the implementation and evaluation of MORSE, documents the research and revisions behind the evolved harness, and provides detailed results and memory examples. It is organized into four appendices: Appendix A: Implementation and Evaluation Protocol. We specify the host interfaces, tool-admission rules, runtime and storage limits, scoring and candidate selection, and the data splits and overlap checks used during evolution and evaluation. Appendix B: Research and Harness Evolution. We trace the Editors literature research across rounds, connect tool requests to the failures that motivated them, summarize the eleven accepted harness updates and their validation results, and examine how accepted updates affect the failures they target and the remaining questions. Appendix C: Additional Quantitative Results. We report latency, write-cost, and prompt-token results, give StreamingBench results by task and backbone, and describe our reproductions of MemEvo, OASIS, and the direct VLM baseline. Appendix D: Memory at Question Time. Three OVOBench examples illustrate what the final harness stores, retrieves, and sends to the answering VLM for episodic recall, action ordering, and future prediction. Throughout this material, the main run is the evolution run with Qwen3-VL-8B analyzed in the main paper, and HS11 is its final harness. A. Implementation and Evaluation Protocol A.1. Host Protocol and Runtime Limits Research access. The Editor uses host-side broker for paper search and reading, searches over released models and code, and page reads from approved documentation hosts. The broker logs requests, enforces the per-round budget Bres, and blocks sources of training, validation, and test data, including benchmark repositories, dataset pages, question-answer annotations, and other answerbearing files. Retrieved material informs candidate development without exposing evaluation content, concern also identified in recursive video-harness optimization [22]. Tool requests and admission. Candidates cannot install executable content from the network or load additional models directly. tool request specifies the model and its interface, the training failures it targets, and how its outputs would enter the harness. It includes the expected per-call latency, license, training-data provenance, and links to the paper and model page. The host excludes models trained or fine-tuned on evaluation videos or annotations and admits only non-generative models, keeping the frozen VLM as the answer generator. An approved service becomes available after the host deploys its backend and registers its interface and timing profile. Requests can remain pending across rounds. Every call counts toward the answer latency or the write load in Eq. (2). Storage and context. The host enforces persistent store of 64 frames and separate 16-second readable window. The four most recent frames required in each answer come from this window and do not use persistent slots. Each VLM call can contain at most 32 frames, leaving at most 28 additional frames in HS11. Cropped images cannot be persisted. Text and vectors have no host-wide storage cap: host captions and the final harnesss segment embeddings can grow with the stream. Other structures use programdefined limits, including 120 step-span notes, 40 chapter notes, and 48 per-frame CLIP vectors in HS11. The host also limits each episode to 20,000 service calls and each call to 131,072 context tokens. A.2. Scoring and Candidate Selection Option probabilities. The scorer finds the last generated token that normalizes to valid option letter, stripping surrounding spaces and the punctuation .():*. At that position, it aggregates the returned top-20 token logprobabilities λi(v) over spelling variants of each valid option a: mi(a) = pi = (cid:88) exp λi(v), vTop20i norm(v)=a mi(yi) (cid:80) mi(a) aOi (8) , where Oi is the set of valid letters. correct option absent from the returned alternatives receives zero mass. If several answer calls record probabilities, the last recorded distribution is used. An answered question without recorded distribution falls back to its binary correctness; unanswered questions receive zero. Latency during evolution. The gates compare candidate with its parent on the same streams, so the latency they use should not vary between repeated runs of the same program. During evolution, we therefore estimate the time of each service call with linear function of its input size, such as the number of frames, texts, and prompt and completion to1 kens, fitted once and kept fixed. Summing these estimates over the calls of question or stream gives the answer latency and write load used by the gates, which are the values shown for each round in Figure 3 and Table 8. These estimates guide candidate screening and selection during evolution. All latency and write-cost results reported for the test benchmarks, including Figure 4, are measured on single NVIDIA H100 GPU. Selection and history. The main run maintains single head. Accuracy selection forms Pareto layers using higher and lower latency, treating latency differences within 2% as equivalent, and takes the largest on the first layer. Points differing by less than 104 in and within 2% in latency are collapsed in pool order: the head first, then current candidates in proposal order, their merges, and finally archived candidates. Efficiency selection excludes the archive and orders eligible current candidates by increasing latency, breaking ties by higher . Training results inform diagnosis but do not determine acceptance. Each round starts new Editor session; diagnosis, planning, editing, and merging within that round share the session. The workspace supplies current code, per-question training traces and histories, aggregate validation scores, previous analysis and edit summaries, candidate diffs, reusable observations, and service admission status. The host retains snapshots of candidates that passed the gate without being selected, for archive selection. The Editor can also apply saved diffs from rejected candidates to copy of the current head and submit the combination as new proposal. This is how rounds 6, 8, 12, and 20 reused earlier candidates. The combined programs underwent engineering checks and validation, passed the gates, and had the highest in their selection pools. The drivers separate merge stage combines only current-round candidates that pass the gate and share parent, then revalidates the resulting programs. A.3. Evaluation Subsets and Data Separation Evolution uses training and validation sets constructed from NExT-GQA [53], STAR [52], ReXTime [7], COIN [41], YouCook2 [72], and the COIN subset of OVBench [13]. The training split contains 780 questions on 370 streams, and validation contains 388 questions on 182 streams. OVO-Bench evaluation includes six real-time perception tasks (OCR, ACR, ATR, STU, FPD, and OJR) and three backward-tracing tasks (EPM, ASI, and HLD), totaling 1,468 questions on 512 videos. We exclude forward active responding. StreamingBench evaluation includes realtime visual understanding, anomalous and misleading contextual understanding, and sequential question answering. Omni-source and proactive-output tasks are excluded. Sequential questions use the official history. Training and validation share no videos, and neither Table 6. B. Research and Harness Evolution B.1. External Research The research broker records every request of the Editor, and the analysis report of each round states what the Editor concluded from the material it read. This section reconstructs the main run from these records. The counts quoted below are the Editors own measurements on training questions. Volume. Over the 25 rounds the broker served 153 requests: 79 literature searches, 53 paper reads, 13 searches of model and code hubs, and 8 page fetches (six model cards or code repositories and two arXiv abstracts). The searches returned 587 results covering 209 distinct papers, and the Editor opened 28 of them  (Table 6)  , in 22 of the 25 rounds. Counting the two abstracts, 50 of the 55 paper reads fall in the accuracy stage. Several papers were consulted repeatedly: VideoAgent [9] and R4DSG [27] six times each, in five rounds each. Eighteen of the 28 papers appeared in 2026 and seven in 2025. 2 Rounds 13: recovering past evidence, and the first tool. The seed answers from captions and the four most recent frames. In round 1 the Editor re-asked the 209 training questions that the seed answered incorrectly with 12 uniformly sampled past frames added: 45 became correct, and for 32 of these the past frames, not the added reasoning step, made the difference. It read Vista [25] and proposed six ways to retain and recall past frames, among them CLIP recall by question, X-CLIP [29] clip scoring, and OWLv2 [28] object frames. All six passed the gate, and their merge raised accuracy by 5.9 points, the largest step of the run. In round 2 it found that 46 incorrect questions about brief handobject interactions are decided by one to three frames and that the VLMs choice flips under neutral rewording in 5 of 23 cases. It searched model hub, located VideoMAE classifier fine-tuned on Something-Somethingv2 [43], read its model card, and requested it. The classifier was installed in round 3, and the action hints built on it passed the gate (0.8 points). In between, round 2 accepted one-sentence change to the answer prompt (2.1 points). The round-3 report also concluded that most remaining errors were not decision errors: the VLM does not see the gold event in its frames, and about three quarters of the confident wrong answers were attributed to perception or label-granularity limit. This diagnosis directed the following rounds toward memory and perception. text memory. Rounds 37: From round 3 the Editor read memory designs for streaming and long video: coverage-driven keyframe selection [70], online textual memory [5], OASIS [20], EventMemAgent [51], VideoAgent [9], WorldMM [60], R4DSG [27], StreamMeCo [46], Event-VStream [11], and SVMemAgent [15]. Informed by these designs, it implemented several text memories: an event log, step log, chapter summaries, and verified event entries. The literature also helped it interpret what it observed. write-time action log missed the deciding interaction on six of six inspected videos and wrote confident wrong lines, which the Editor related to the confabulation effect reported in [64]. An always-on event log fixed 24 training questions but broke 21, the distractor effect of retrieving more text reported in [5]. From these it derived two rules for the rounds that followed: to write few, verified, specific entries and to retrieve less. Designs that need services the host does not provide, such as the tracking and segmentation of R4DSG, or that exceed the latency and write budgets, such as the multi-turn retrieval of WorldMM, were set aside. Chapter summaries entered the accepted harness in round 6 as part of merge. Rounds 811: perception aids. In round 8 the Editor found that, for handobject questions, the asked object was not visible to the VLM at the Solvers frame size in five of eight inspected wrong cases, against one of five correct It read Divide, then Ground [18], Think While controls. Watching [47], and Video-EM [50], concluded that text entries need faithfulness checks rather than more entries, and requested handobject contact detector [38] and regioncrop operation. Region crop was installed in round 9. In that round the Editor read study of visual cropping [68], which reports that accuracy depends on the size of the visual subject and that sending crop with the full image helps, and proposed detector-guided crops that follow this recipe. In round 10 it observed that the scene often stays unchanged when step ends, so whole-frame change points miss the end, and requested RAFT optical flow [42] as hand-region motion signal, which was installed in round 11. These two services were explored without entering the accepted harness  (Table 7)  . Rounds 1015: fine-grained step log. An anchor-based step-log hint was proposed in round 10 but fell below the probability gate. In round 11, reading VideoAgent, VideoEM, Visual Agentic Memory [16], MM-Mem [19], online textual memory [5], and R4DSG informed further experiments. Training counterexamples showed that the hint could recommend the wrong option or be ignored. The Editor therefore tested short excerpt of the anchor and its next two log entries in place of an explicit option recommendation, choice also supported by Video-EM and online textual memory. Trigger and anchor adjustments came from training-set calibration. Neither this excerpt variant nor separate duration-oriented ledger passed the gate. The combination accepted in round 12 reused the round-10 step-log code unchanged. Round 12 read Glance and Focus [4] as the closest published design to anchor localization, and the confabulation study motivated candidate that checks caption claims against the detector. In rounds 1315 the Editor read keyframe-selection and streaming-memory methods, including Adaptive Keyframe Sampling [40], ReQuest [14], and ProV-Mem [45], and tested their premise on its own traces: is flat in the share of held evidence that is sent (0.766, 0.754, and 0.777).
